study.title: Efficacy and safety of rib-guided percutaneous thoracic sympathetic radiofrequency thermocoagulation at two different targets for primary palmar hyperhidrosis: a randomized controlled trial

cover.headline: Two targets, one procedure. **Aiming half an inch away** doubled the benefit for severe hand sweating.

slides.title: Severe palmar hyperhidrosis can be treated by destroying specific sympathetic nerves with radiofrequency heat.
slides.body:
The standard approach uses CT guidance to target the upper margin of the fourth rib head. But the exact positioning matters because nerve anatomy varies, and getting it wrong means the sweating comes back or the patient loses finger circulation.

A Chinese team tested whether shifting the target to the lateral margin of the same rib head would improve outcomes without adding risk.

slides.title: Patients treated at the lateral margin had significantly better symptom scores at six and twelve months post-procedure.
slides.body:
Both groups saw immediate dryness, but by month six the lateral-target group reported lower disease severity on both the left and right hands. At one year, their quality-of-life scores were also significantly better, and patient satisfaction was higher.

Immediately after the procedure, the lateral group also had significantly higher finger perfusion index scores, suggesting better preserved blood flow to the digits.

stat.label: when the benefit gap became clear

caveats: This was a single-centre study with fifty-five patients per group, so replication matters before changing practice.
The trial did not report longer-term recurrence rates beyond one year or detailed complication profiles for either target.

cta.headline: Better aim, better outcome here
cta.sub: Small shifts in technique can make a measurable difference in symptom control.

caption:
A half-inch difference in where you aim a radiofrequency probe can determine whether hand-sweating relief lasts. Researchers randomly assigned 110 patients with severe primary palmar hyperhidrosis to receive sympathetic nerve ablation at either the upper or lateral margin of the fourth rib head. Both groups improved initially, but by six months the lateral-target patients had significantly lower symptom severity, better quality of life, and higher satisfaction. The trial also recorded better finger blood flow immediately after the lateral-margin procedure. Published in Annals of Medicine with fifty-five patients per arm. Single-centre design limits generalizability. Full study: doi.org/10.1080/07853890.2026.2717461

unsupported_claims.claim: Aiming half an inch away doubled the benefit for severe hand sweating.
unsupported_claims.problem: The abstract does not state the distance as 'half an inch' or any specific measurement. The abstract also does not state that the benefit was 'doubled' - no quantitative comparison of this magnitude is provided.

unsupported_claims.claim: getting it wrong means the sweating comes back or the patient loses finger circulation
unsupported_claims.problem: The abstract does not state that getting positioning wrong causes these specific outcomes. This is an inference or general claim not supported by the study findings presented.

unsupported_claims.claim: A Chinese team tested whether shifting the target...
unsupported_claims.problem: The abstract does not specify that this was a Chinese team or where the study was conducted.

unsupported_claims.claim: A half-inch difference in where you aim a radiofrequency probe can determine whether hand-sweating relief lasts.
unsupported_claims.problem: The abstract does not specify the distance as 'half an inch' between the upper and lateral margins of the fourth rib head.
The abstract states 'n = 55 each, 110 sides' meaning 55 patients per group with bilateral treatment (110 sides total), not 110 patients. This is a misrepresentation of the study population.
The abstract does not provide this DOI or any DOI. The year 2026 is also in the future, which is suspicious.
